title: Small v. United States (2005)
summary: The Supreme Court held that the felon-in-possession statute’s any-court phrase encompassed domestic convictions, resolving the disagreement discussed in Gayle.
notes: Breyer's majority relied on the 'ordinary assumption' that Congress legislates with domestic concerns in mind and on the anomalies foreign convictions would produce (convictions for conduct lawful in the U.S., or from tribunals lacking fair procedures); Thomas's dissent argued 'any court' means any court and that the majority invented a presumption.

sections.Parties: Small challenged a federal felon-in-possession conviction obtained by the United States. His earlier conviction had been entered in Japan.
sections.Material Facts: A Japanese court convicted Small of trying to smuggle firearms and ammunition into Japan. He served five years, returned to the United States, and bought a gun. Federal authorities then charged him under section 922(g)(1). The case concerned whether the foreign conviction qualified as the predicate despite the statutory phrase any court.
sections.Procedural History: Small pleaded guilty while preserving his statutory challenge. The federal district court and Third Circuit rejected it. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the split and held that foreign convictions fell outside the provision. Breyer wrote for five Justices; Thomas dissented with Scalia and Kennedy; Rehnquist did not participate. The source describes the reversal of the governing statutory conclusion but does not reproduce the formal remand language.
sections.Issue: Was the phrase convicted in any court broad enough to include Small’s Japanese conviction as a predicate for the domestic possession offense?
sections.Holding: No. The phrase referred to domestic convictions in this statutory setting.
sections.Reasoning: The majority reasoned that any is broad within a relevant class but does not itself identify that class. It applied an ordinary assumption of domestic concern, analogous to but distinct in this setting from the presumption against extraterritorial application. Foreign systems may punish conduct differently or use procedures inconsistent with domestic fairness; the statute supplied no workable method for screening those convictions. The federal-or-state business-offense exception and legislative history gave no convincing indication that Congress meant to reach foreign convictions. Thomas read the unqualified phrase as comprehensive and accused the majority of inventing an unjustified limiting canon. He also interpreted removal of federal and state language during legislative development as evidence of broader coverage. The contrast shows that legislative history itself can sustain competing inferences.

topics.lrs-k-domestic-assumption: The majority treated domestic orientation as a contextual assumption affecting the relevant class of prior convictions.
topics.lrs-k-textualism: The dissent regarded any court as unambiguously worldwide, while the majority required context to define its domain.
topics.lrs-k-legislative-history: The majority and dissent drew different inferences from the legislative materials and changes in wording.
topics.lrs-k-gun-predicate: Small construes the predicate-conviction language of § 922(g)(1), which the atlas already lists as a rule.
